{{short description|American statistician}}
'''Rosedith Sitgreaves Bowker''' (1915 – February 1, 1992) was an American [[statistician]] who taught at [[Columbia University]] and [[Stanford University]].<ref name="wp">{{citation|title=Rosedith Sitgreaves Bowker, Statistics Professor|newspaper=[[Washington Post]]|date=February 4, 1992|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1992/02/04/luigi-petrullo-psychologist-dies/6ecc6eec-15d1-45fe-8e47-cd988a9b7679/}}.</ref> Her publications included research on [[random matrix|random matrices]] and [[Kendall's W]].

Rosedith Sitgreaves was born in [[Easton, Pennsylvania]]. She did her undergraduate studies at [[Wilson College (Pennsylvania)|Wilson College]], a women's college in Pennsylvania. She earned a master's degree from [[George Washington University]] and a doctorate from [[Columbia University]], both in statistical mathematics.<ref name="wp"/> Her doctoral dissertation was entitled ''Contributions to the Problem of Classification''.<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=50551}}</ref> When she completed it, in 1953, she became the first female doctoral graduate of Columbia's statistics program.<ref name="cu">{{citation
 | last1 = Zheng | first1 = Tian | author1-link = Tian Zheng
 | last2 = Ying | first2 = Zhiliang
 | contribution = Columbia University Statistics
 | mr = 3077323
 | pages = 27–38
 | publisher = Springer, New York
 | title = Strength in numbers: the rising of academic statistics departments in the U.S
 | year = 2013}}. See in particular [https://books.google.com/books?id=kPGJUiUCJZkC&pg=PA35 p.&nbsp;35].</ref>

Sitgreaves worked at the [[United States Public Health Service]] from 1943 to 1953. After completing her doctorate, she worked as a research associate at [[Stanford University]], and then returned to Columbia as a faculty member in education and statistics.<ref name="wp"/> In this period, in 1964, she married [[Albert H. Bowker]], a fellow graduate of the Columbia statistics program<ref name="cu"/> who at the time was chancellor of the [[City University of New York]] and president of the [[American Statistical Association]], as his second wife.<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/09/27/miss-sitgreaves-and-dr-bowker-marry-in-easton.html|title=Miss Sitgreaves And Dr. Bowker Marry in Easton|date=September 27, 1964|newspaper=[[New York Times]]}}.</ref> Although she used the name "Rosedith Sitgreaves Bowker" in social settings, she continued to use "Rosedith Sitgreaves" as her name for her publications and professional affiliations.

In 1971, the Bowkers moved to California: Al Bowker became chancellor of the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and Sitgreaves taught at [[California State University, East Bay]] and then in the school of education at [[Stanford University]].<ref name="wp"/> As a woman with her own academic career, she gave UC Berkeley "its first experience of a Chancellor's wife who served successfully as official hostess without sacrificing her professional work" and "opened new possibilities for the spouses of subsequent Chancellors to shape their own roles".<ref>[http://content.cdlib.org/view?docId=hb1p3001qq&doc.view=entire_text Sixth Chancellor, University Of California, Berkeley, 1971-1980; Statistician, and National Leader in the Policies and Politics of Higher Education], University of California, retrieved 2016-07-19.</ref> After she and her husband retired in 1980, they moved to the [[Washington, DC]] area in 1980, where Sitgreaves worked for the [[U.S. National Institute of Education|National Institute of Education]].<ref name="wp"/>

In 1960 she was elected as a [[Fellow]] of the [[American Statistical Association]].<ref>[http://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm List of ASA Fellows] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160616161612/https://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm |date=2016-06-16 }}, retrieved 2016-07-19.</ref>
